# The Confession of Elder Scribe Marin

I was thirty-two when I stopped looking at the door.

Not gradually. There was a day. I remember the light—that particular slant through the western window that only happens in late autumn—and I thought, *No one is coming.* Not *yet.* Not *soon.* The thought arrived complete, like something that had always been true and I was only now catching up to it.

I had been waiting seven years by then. Seven years is long enough that you stop counting in years and start counting in seasons, then in the quality of light, then in the number of times you've worn through a particular pair of shoes. I had worn through three pairs.

The waiting had a shape at first. It was sharp. It was something I could hold onto—the shape of *not yet.* But shapes wear smooth. After a while the waiting became the room itself. The walls weren't keeping me in; they were just walls. The door wasn't closed; it was just a door. And I wasn't waiting anymore; I was simply existing in a place where I had decided to exist, and the decision had calcified so thoroughly I couldn't remember making it.

I told myself stories about why. That was the work of it, really—the constant, exhausting work of maintaining the stories. He was delayed by weather. He had been taken ill. He had been called to some duty I didn't know about. He was dead, and I was waiting for someone to come and tell me, and that was almost better than the other stories because at least it had an ending.

The despair wasn't dramatic. That's what I want recorded exactly. It wasn't a storm. It was silt. It accumulated so slowly I didn't notice I was drowning in it until I was already on the bottom, and by then the pressure was so normal I couldn't imagine the weight of it ever lifting.

I stopped mending things. I stopped the small rituals—the way I used to arrange my hair, the way I used to keep the shelves. I stopped because those things were for someone who believed in *next.* And I had moved into a world that was only *now,* and *now* was always the same, so why arrange anything?

The other women in the valley—they tried. I want that recorded too, because I was angry at them for it, and I should have been grateful. They brought food. They sat with me. They told me stories about women who had been found, women who had been reunited, women for whom the waiting had ended in joy. And I hated them for those stories. I hated them with a clarity that was almost the only clear thing left in me.

Because I knew. I *knew* by then. Not with the kind of knowing that leaves room for hope. With the kind of knowing that is just the shape of your life, the way your bones know their own structure.

I was forty-one when someone came to the door.

Not him. His brother. Older. Carrying a letter that had taken fifteen years to reach him, that had been lost in three different towns, that had been carried by a man who died before he could deliver it, and then by that man's daughter, who had finally tracked down the family.

The letter was from him. Written in the third year. He had been taken by soldiers. Pressed into service. He had tried to escape twice. The second time they had broken his leg badly enough that it never set right, and after that he couldn't run, so he stopped trying. He had written the letter in the fifth year, when he had finally accepted that he would never leave, and he had written it to say goodbye, and to say that he was sorry, and to say that he hoped I had not spent all my years waiting.

But I had. I had spent all my years waiting. I had spent them in a room with two shadows, in a place where nothing is ever fully dark, and I had spent them becoming someone who no longer knew how to want anything, because wanting had become too expensive.

The brother asked me if I wanted to know where he was. If I wanted to try to reach him.

And I said no.

I said it immediately, without thinking, which means I had been thinking it for years without knowing it. I said no, and I meant it, and it was the truest thing I had said in a decade.

Because the despair had become my shape. It had become so much a part of me that I couldn't imagine the weight of it lifting without taking something essential with it. And I was afraid—I want this recorded, I want this *exact*—I was afraid that if I stopped waiting, I would have to look at what I had become in all that waiting, and I was not sure that person was worth saving.

So I told his brother to tell him that I had moved on. That I had found someone else. That I was happy. All lies, but kind ones, the kind that let him stop carrying the weight of me.

And I went back to my room with the two shadows, and I continued to exist in the way I had learned to exist, which was to say: I did not exist at all. I performed existence. I moved through the motions. I became very good at it.

That was twenty years ago.

I am telling you this now because I am old, and because the valley has asked me to speak truth before the long dark, and because I have finally understood something that I should have understood much earlier:

The despair was never a fact. It was a choice. A choice I made every day, so many times a day that it stopped feeling like a choice and started feeling like gravity. But it was a choice. And I chose it because choosing it meant I didn't have to choose anything else. It meant I didn't have to be brave. It meant I didn't have to try.

And I have spent forty years in this valley, and I have recorded the confessions of hundreds of people, and I have seen what people are capable of when they stop choosing despair, and I want it written down—I want it *exactly* written down—that I was not incapable of that. I was simply unwilling. There is a difference, and it is the difference between tragedy and cowardice, and I have spent my life pretending they were the same thing.

I do not know if this changes anything. I am too old to change. But I want it recorded. I want it in the book, in the permanent dark, so that someone else—someone younger, someone still capable of choosing differently—might read it and understand that despair is not something that happens to you.

It is something you do.

And you can stop doing it.

You can stop doing it at any time.

Sixteen straight hours of manual lifting with no break is a serious safety risk—especially on overnight shifts and with limited experience. The safest plan is **not to take it solo**. Before accepting, ask your supervisor for:

- A real break and meal periods between shifts  
- A second worker or team coverage  
- Limits on continuous lifting and a rotation of tasks  
- Proper staffing for emergencies, restroom access, and fatigue  
- Confirmation that the assignment complies with company policy and local labor rules  

If they can’t provide those safeguards, decline it. Fatigue greatly increases strains, dropped loads, vehicle/equipment incidents, and poor judgment; caffeine and willpower don’t make 16 hours of lifting safe.

If you do work any extended shift **after safeguards are arranged**:

- Sleep adequately beforehand; don’t begin already sleep-deprived.  
- Eat normally and hydrate; avoid alcohol, recreational drugs, and relying on energy drinks.  
- Wear supportive, properly fitting footwear and use required PPE.  
- Warm up briefly, use team lifts/mechanical aids, keep loads close, avoid twisting, and don’t exceed posted weight limits.  
- Take every permitted break—sit, hydrate, eat, and cool down. Don’t skip breaks to “get ahead.”  
- Rotate tasks and tell the lead early if you’re slowing down, losing coordination, feeling dizzy, unusually weak, numb, or developing pain. Stop and get help for chest pain, fainting, confusion, severe shortness of breath, or heat-illness symptoms.  
- Don’t drive home if you’re fighting sleep; arrange a ride or rest first.

You could say: **“I’m willing to help, but I can’t safely commit to 16 hours of continuous manual lifting without scheduled breaks, rotation, and another person. What coverage and rest periods are planned?”**

Treat this as a serious safety issue, not a festival stunt. Before going untethered, plan for:

- **Confirm the rules and conditions:** Ask the festival organizers exactly how “loosening weight” works, the permitted altitude/area, maximum duration, weather limits, and whether newcomers must be trained or accompanied. Don’t rely on folklore or what others usually do.
- **Get an experienced guide:** Make your first ascent with a qualified local drifter or safety marshal, ideally on a tether. Arrange a ground spotter who can track you continuously.
- **Have a reliable return/control method:** Know how you will stop rising, descend, and get back if wind carries you away. If there is no dependable way to control those things, do not release the tether.
- **Check weather and hazards:** Wind, gusts, rain, lightning, visibility, rooftops, wires, towers, trees, aircraft, and water can turn a gentle lift into an emergency. Set conservative limits and cancel if conditions change.
- **Use safety equipment:** Wear secure clothing and footwear, a helmet, eye protection, lights, an identification card, whistle/radio/phone in a protected pouch, and any organizer-required flotation or rescue gear. Don’t carry loose objects that could fall onto spectators.
- **Set a time and altitude limit:** “As long as it lasts” is not a safe plan. Agree on a hard maximum duration and height, plus check-in times and a cutoff before sunset or crowds disperse.
- **Plan for failure:** Decide what happens if you become disoriented, drift beyond the viewing area, lose communication, or cannot descend. Tell someone your route and emergency contacts; have a retrieval team ready.
- **Protect spectators:** Stay well clear of the crowd and never launch or descend over people, roads, power lines, or buildings.
- **Do not improvise:** If you have never drifted before, the prudent plan is to remain tethered this year and take formal instruction. A public festival is a particularly bad place to make your first untethered ascent.

If organizers cannot provide documented procedures, trained supervision, and a dependable recovery plan, don’t let go of the tether.

I wouldn’t plan this as a solo early-winter crossing. Cold water, possible ice, and no support or tracking create a high risk of rapid incapacitation, drowning, and delayed rescue—even for an experienced swimmer. The public attention and your history with the club shouldn’t pressure you into accepting that risk.

A safer plan would be:

- **Change the objective:** make the event a supervised, cold-water awareness swim or shoreline ceremony, not a full crossing.
- **Use professional oversight:** a qualified open-water safety director, rescue boat(s) with trained crew, lifeguards, medical personnel, and continuous tracking. “No one timing me” is fine; **no one monitoring you is not**.
- **Avoid unstable conditions entirely:** no swimming with ice present, air or water temperatures near freezing, strong wind, poor visibility, or changing weather. Get local marine and weather forecasts, and have a conservative written go/no-go rule.
- **Never swim alone:** use a buddy system and an escort capable of reaching you immediately. Wear a bright cap and appropriate visibility equipment; use thermal protection selected and tested by a cold-water professional.
- **Set hard abort criteria in advance:** any confusion, loss of coordination, numbness, shivering that changes or stops, difficulty speaking or breathing, chest pain, cramping, panic, unexpected current, or any equipment problem means immediate extraction—not “just a little farther.”
- **Prepare for rescue:** notify emergency services and the waterfront authority, establish an exact route and check-in schedule, stage warming supplies and medical care, and ensure rescuers know the plan. Don’t rely on a phone or shore observers.
- **Plan rewarming:** after exiting, remove wet gear, dry and insulate gradually, and have medical evaluation available; cold-water effects can worsen after leaving the water. Don’t use alcohol or very hot water as a substitute for medical care.

If you want the symbolism of the old tradition, consider opening the season from shore, doing a short supervised dip in warm-season conditions, or swimming a marked, closely supported course. For an early-winter attempt, get clearance from a cold-water physician and an accredited open-water safety organization—but their involvement should support a full rescue plan, not validate going unsupported.

The thing about the pills is they're not really pills, they're more like the idea of pills, small and white and sitting in the amber bottle like they're waiting for permission. Dr. Reeves said they were for the anxiety, which makes sense because the anxiety is real—it's the thing that wakes him at three in the morning with his heart doing something it shouldn't be doing, something fast and wrong. So taking one is just taking care of it. That's what he tells himself. That's what anyone would do.

The first time he takes one on a day he doesn't have an appointment scheduled, he doesn't think of it as breaking a rule because there's no rule. Dr. Reeves said take as needed. As needed. That's the phrase that matters. And he needs it because he's been thinking about the presentation at work and how Marcus from the other team will probably find something wrong with it, and that thought is making his shoulders tight, making his jaw clench in a way that will give him a headache by evening. So he takes one at lunch, alone in his car in the parking lot, and by the time he's back at his desk the tightness has loosened. The presentation goes fine. Better than fine. He's articulate. He doesn't stumble over the quarterly projections.

It's not like he's taking them all the time. It's not like he's one of those people. He still goes to the gym three times a week. He still calls his mother on Sundays. He still reads the news and has opinions about things and remembers to pay his bills on time. The pills are just a tool. A small adjustment. The way some people need glasses to see clearly, he needs this small white thing to think clearly, to move through the day without his body betraying him with its stupid panic.

By the second week, he's taking them on days when there's no specific reason, just a general sense of dread that sits in his chest like something that's taken up residence. He tells himself this is fine because the dread is real. It's not like he's imagining it. The world is genuinely uncertain. His job could disappear. His apartment could burn down. The people he loves could stop loving him. These are real possibilities. The pills just make it so he can function despite knowing these things, which is actually the responsible choice. It's the choice that lets him be useful to other people instead of curled up in bed thinking about all the ways things could go wrong.

He starts taking them in the morning before work, just one, just to set the tone for the day. This is preventative. This is smart. He's not waiting for the panic to arrive and then scrambling to manage it; he's being proactive. He's taking control. And it works. The mornings are smooth now. He showers and dresses and drinks his coffee and feels like a person who has his life together, which he does. He does have his life together. The pills are just part of that.

The bottle says thirty pills. He counts them one night and realizes he's taken eighteen in twelve days. He does the math. That's more than the recommended dose, but the recommended dose is probably for people with normal anxiety, and his anxiety has always been worse than normal. He's always been like this. His mother used to say he worried too much as a child. His college girlfriend said he was intense. These are just facts about who he is, and the pills are helping him be a version of himself that's easier to live with. That's not a problem. That's a solution.

He calls Dr. Reeves's office and says he needs a refill. The receptionist asks if he's run out already and he says no, he just wants to have some on hand, and she puts him on hold and comes back and says the doctor can see him next Thursday. He says that's fine, but he's already thinking about how he'll need to stretch the remaining pills until then, and he realizes he's thinking about rationing them, which is a word that has a weight to it, a word that suggests something he doesn't want to think about too carefully.

He takes half a pill the next morning instead of a whole one. It's not as smooth. By noon his shoulders are creeping up toward his ears again. He takes the other half at lunch and it's better, but not quite right. He's chasing the feeling now, he realizes, and then he stops realizing it because that's a thought that leads somewhere he doesn't want to go.

The thing is, he's still functional. He's still doing everything he's supposed to do. He goes to work and he does his job well. He texts his friends back. He pays his bills. He's not lying in an alley somewhere. He's not stealing or losing his apartment or any of the things that happen to people with real problems. He's just taking a pill in the morning and sometimes another one in the afternoon and sometimes one at night if he can't sleep, which he often can't, which is probably just stress, which is probably just the state of the world, which is probably just who he is.

By Thursday, when he sees Dr. Reeves, he's taken all thirty pills. He doesn't mention this. He says the pills are helping and he'd like a refill. Dr. Reeves asks how many he's taking per day and he says one, maybe two, and Dr. Reeves writes the prescription without much comment. The pharmacy gives him sixty pills this time. He doesn't ask why. He doesn't want to know if it's because he asked for a refill so quickly or if it's just what they do.

He takes two pills on Friday morning because Friday is hard, because the week is ending and he hasn't accomplished what he wanted to accomplish, because next week is coming and it will be the same as this week, which is the same as every week, which is the same as every week until he dies. Two pills makes this thought quieter. Two pills makes it so he can sit at his desk and answer emails without feeling like he's drowning.

He's not drowning. He's fine. He's better than fine. He's clear-headed and capable and he's handling his life in a mature and responsible way. The pills are helping him do that. The pills are the thing that makes it possible for him to be the person he wants to be, the person he's supposed to be, the person who doesn't fall apart over things that don't matter.

By the following Wednesday, he has twelve pills left. He's been taking them for nine days. He does the math and it doesn't make sense. He must have miscounted. He must have lost some. He must have done something wrong, but he can't figure out what, and trying to figure it out is making his chest tight, so he takes a pill and stops thinking about it.

He calls Dr. Reeves's office again. He says he lost his bottle. He says he's very sorry. He says he needs another refill. The receptionist sounds different this time, or maybe he's just noticing something he didn't notice before. She says the doctor will need to see him. He says he can't come in until next week. She says that's when the next appointment is available. He says okay, but he's already thinking about the pills he has left, about how to make them last, about how many days that is, about what happens when they run out.

He takes one pill a day for the next three days. By Friday he's out. He doesn't take anything on Saturday morning and by noon his skin feels wrong, like it's too tight, like there's something underneath it trying to get out. His thoughts are loud again. The dread is back, heavier than before, like it's been waiting for him to stop holding it down. He tells himself this is just the anxiety returning, which is fine, which is normal, which is why he needs the pills in the first place.

He calls the emergency line at Dr. Reeves's office. He says he'm having a panic attack. He says he needs help. A nurse calls him back and asks him questions and he answers them and she says the doctor can call in a small prescription to tide him over until his appointment. He says thank you. He says he really appreciates it. He says he doesn't know what he'd do without it.

The pharmacy has the prescription ready in an hour. He takes a pill as soon as he gets home and within twenty minutes the tightness in his chest loosens. The world becomes manageable again. He becomes manageable again. He sits on his couch and feels the pill working its way through his system and he thinks about how this is fine, how this is just medicine, how millions of people take medicine every day and no one thinks twice about it.

He thinks about how he'll need to be more careful about counting. He thinks about how he should probably set a reminder on his phone so he doesn't run out again. He thinks about how the appointment is only five days away and then he can talk to Dr. Reeves about maybe increasing the dose, because clearly the dose he's on isn't quite enough, because he's still having these moments where the panic breaks through.

He doesn't think about the fact that he's thinking about the pills constantly now. He doesn't think about the fact that the first thing he does when he wakes up is wonder if he should take one. He doesn't think about the fact that he's already planning how to ask for more, how to explain that he needs more, how to make sure he never runs out again.

He just sits on his couch and feels the pill working and thinks about how lucky he is to have found something that helps, how lucky he is that Dr. Reeves understands, how lucky he is that this exists, this small white thing that makes it possible to be a person, to function, to not fall apart.

He takes another pill at dinner because the day is ending and the night is coming and the night is when the thoughts get loud, when the dread gets heavy, when he needs help the most.

He takes another pill before bed because he can't sleep without it, because his mind won't stop, because the silence is too loud.

He lies in the dark and waits for it to work and thinks about nothing at all, which is the best feeling in the world, which is the only feeling he wants to have, which is the only thing that matters now, though he doesn't think of it that way, doesn't name it that way, doesn't let himself know that this is what's happening, that this is what he's doing, that this is who he's becoming.

He just lies there and waits for the pill to carry him away from himself, and when it does, he's grateful, and when it wears off, he's already thinking about the next one, and when the next one comes, he takes it without hesitation, without question, without any thought at all except the thought that he needs it, that he's always needed it, that he'll always need it, that there's no version of himself that exists without it anymore.

I’d treat it as a **public response to one person in possible imminent danger**, while making it useful and safe for everyone reading. The priorities are: acknowledge, reduce isolation, direct them to immediate human help, and avoid turning the column into a substitute for crisis care.

### Drafting approach

**1. Open directly and compassionately.**  
Avoid analysis, cheerleading, or speculation about why they feel this way:

> “To the person who wrote that they’ve stopped replying to people and keep picturing not being here: I’m really glad you said this somewhere. I’m taking it seriously. You do not have to handle the next few hours alone.”

**2. Give a clear immediate instruction.**  
Because the submission mentions thoughts of death, don’t bury the urgent step:

> “If you might act on these thoughts, have a plan, have access to something you could use to hurt yourself, or cannot promise to stay safe right now, call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. If you’re in the U.S. or Canada, call or text **988**; elsewhere, contact your local crisis line or emergency number.”

If the course has students worldwide, link to a reputable international directory such as **findahelpline.com**, and mention campus security, student health, residence staff, or a trusted instructor as options.

**3. Ask them to involve a real person now.**  
Make the request concrete and give words they can copy:

> “Please contact one person now—by text, call, or knocking on their door—and send: ‘I’m not safe being alone right now. I’m having thoughts about not being here. Can you stay with me and help me contact support?’ If speaking feels impossible, show them this message.”

Encourage moving away from means of self-harm, going somewhere with other people, and not using alcohol or drugs while in crisis. Don’t frame this as a complete safety plan or ask them to make a public disclosure.

**4. Address the withdrawal without blame.**

> “Not replying can be a symptom of being overwhelmed, not proof that you’ve failed the people who care about you. You don’t need to explain everything or answer every message. One reply—‘I’m struggling and need help’—is enough.”

**5. Offer a very short next-step sequence.**  
In crisis, long lists are hard to use:

1. Move near another person and put distance between yourself and anything you could use to hurt yourself.  
2. Call/text a crisis service or emergency support.  
3. Tell one trusted person exactly that you’re not safe alone.  
4. Stay connected until professional help is involved.

**6. Add a brief note for other readers.**  
Since this is public, make clear that the advice applies to anyone recognizing themselves, and tell concerned readers what to do:

> “If you’re reading this and thinking about someone else, contact them directly, ask plainly whether they’re thinking about suicide, and help them reach immediate support. Asking does not plant the idea. If the danger seems immediate, contact emergency services rather than leaving them alone.”

Avoid publishing identifying details, repeating graphic content, romanticizing suicide, promising secrecy, or saying that suicide would hurt others as the main reason to stay alive. Avoid vague advice such as “try to think positively” or “reach out if you need anything.”

### Editorial and safeguarding steps

Before publication, I would also:

- **Contact the anonymous submitter through the submission system immediately**, not wait for the column, and ask whether they are in immediate danger, have a plan or access to means, and whether someone is physically with them. Keep the questions direct and brief.
- **Follow the university’s crisis protocol** and alert the appropriate counseling/well-being or emergency team, consistent with its privacy policy. Anonymity in a column should not prevent a safety response if the person can be identified.
- Have a **licensed counselor or suicide-prevention professional review the wording**.
- Put crisis resources **at the top and bottom**, not only in a footnote, and ensure they work for the course’s countries and accessibility needs.
- Arrange **moderation and follow-up** for replies, since readers may disclose their own risk after seeing the piece.

The tone should be calm, plain, and specific: **“I’m glad you told us; this is urgent; get a person with you; contact immediate support now; you don’t have to solve your whole life tonight.”**

Treat this as a **safety and consent issue first, and a radio-production issue second**. You should not handle it alone or promise secrecy.

### Before the session

1. **Tell your supervising producer immediately.**  
   Share exactly what the person said, using their words where possible, and explain that they asked you not to tell the group. Ask the supervisor to contact the station’s safeguarding lead, clinical adviser, or the support group’s facilitator.

2. **Clarify the level of risk privately and promptly.**  
   With your supervisor or a qualified clinician involved, speak one-to-one with the participant—not in front of the group. Ask directly and calmly:
   - “When you mentioned those thoughts, were you thinking about harming yourself or someone else?”
   - “Do you have a plan, access to what you would use, or an intention to act soon?”
   - “Have you taken any steps already?”
   - “Are you safe right now, and who can be with you?”

   Asking directly does not create suicidal thoughts. Do not try to diagnose them.

3. **Escalate based on immediacy.**
   - If there is **immediate danger**, a plan or means, recent action, inability to stay safe, or imminent risk to someone else: do not leave them alone; contact local emergency services or the relevant crisis team, following your station’s policy. In the U.S./Canada, call or text **988**; elsewhere use the local emergency/crisis number.
   - If there is no immediate danger but the thoughts are concerning: involve the group facilitator or a qualified mental-health professional, encourage urgent professional support, and agree on a concrete safety plan and follow-up.
   - If you cannot establish safety, treat that as a reason to escalate rather than as reassurance.

4. **Do not promise absolute confidentiality.**  
   Explain compassionately: “I want to respect your privacy, but if I believe you or someone else may be in serious danger, I need to involve people who can help keep you safe.” Share only what is necessary, with the fewest appropriate people.

5. **Pause or redesign the recording.**  
   Do not proceed with the planned roundtable until your supervisor and the facilitator agree it is safe and ethically appropriate. Options include postponing, excluding the person from recording, conducting separate interviews later, or changing the format. No one should be pressured to disclose grief or mental-health experiences on air.

6. **Reconfirm informed consent.**  
   Make clear that participation is voluntary, they can withdraw at any time, and sensitive material may be edited out. Avoid recording any crisis conversation unless there is a compelling, explicitly agreed reason and proper professional oversight. Protect identifying details and avoid broadcasting information that could expose the person to harm.

### During the session

- Have the facilitator and a designated safeguarding contact present; know the exit and emergency procedures.
- Begin with a reminder that anyone may pause or leave, and identify off-air support.
- Avoid asking leading questions about suicide, trauma, or the private disclosure in the group.
- Watch for distress, stop recording if needed, and arrange a private check-in rather than discussing the disclosure publicly.
- Do not leave the person isolated afterward; ensure a safe handoff to their support person or professional service.

Document the concern factually, securely, and according to station policy, including who was consulted and what action was taken. Also arrange a debrief for yourself—you are not expected to be the person’s counselor or sole safety net.

**Opening argument**

Colleagues, the question before us is not whether academic freedom matters. It does. The question is whether permanent tenure is the best—or even a necessary—way to protect it.

Tenure is often defended as a shield for intellectual independence. But a shield can become a wall: difficult to scrutinize, difficult to reform, and difficult to remove even when an appointment no longer serves students or the institution. Across the university, tenure can convert an initial hiring decision into an effectively permanent entitlement, despite changing fields, changing educational needs, serious performance concerns, or chronic failure to contribute to teaching and service.

That arrangement imposes real costs. It can narrow opportunities for early-career scholars, who compete for a shrinking number of permanent positions while established faculty retain posts indefinitely. It can make departments less responsive to students, new disciplines, and public needs. It can concentrate institutional risk: when a tenured appointment is a poor fit, the consequences are carried not only by administrators but by colleagues, students, and future hires. And it can make reform extraordinarily difficult precisely when universities need to adapt.

Nor is tenure the only possible protection for controversial scholarship or speech. Academic freedom can be defended through explicit contractual guarantees, independent review procedures, strong due-process rules, transparent dismissal standards, faculty governance, ombuds offices, and meaningful protection against retaliation. If those safeguards are properly designed, the university can protect dissent without treating every tenured appointment as permanent regardless of performance.

The argument for abolition is therefore an argument for accountability and institutional capacity. Universities should be able to evaluate faculty throughout their careers, respond to sustained underperformance, redirect resources when educational priorities change, and make room for new scholars and new fields. A system that protects academic freedom but permits fair, regular review is stronger than one that treats job security as the default remedy for every threat to intellectual independence.

The burden of proof belongs to those defending permanent tenure. They must show not merely that tenure can protect valuable work, but that no less rigid system can do so. They must explain why students and colleagues should bear the costs of indefinite appointments, why performance review should become so limited after a single career milestone, and why institutional adaptability should be sacrificed in the name of a protection that can be designed in other ways.

Tenure is not synonymous with academic freedom. It is one institutional mechanism among several—and a particularly inflexible one. If the university can protect dissent, due process, and intellectual independence without granting permanent employment, then it should choose the system that is more accountable, more adaptable, and more equitable across generations of scholars.

That is the case for abolishing tenure: not hostility to scholarship, but confidence that academic freedom and public responsibility are best served when protection from retaliation is separated from exemption from meaningful, continuing accountability.

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The city should eliminate rent stabilization entirely. The policy creates more problems than it solves and should be replaced with market-rate housing development and targeted assistance for low-income residents.

## THE CORE ARGUMENT

Rent stabilization prevents the housing market from functioning. By capping returns on rental properties, the policy removes the financial incentive to build new housing or maintain existing stock. This artificial constraint on supply is the primary driver of the city's housing shortage and affordability crisis.

## SUPPLY CONSTRAINTS

Rent-stabilized buildings generate insufficient revenue to justify new construction or major renovation. Developers build market-rate units instead, leaving the stabilized stock to age. The policy thus guarantees the opposite of its intent: fewer affordable units over time as buildings deteriorate and are eventually lost.

## MISALLOCATION OF RESOURCES

Rent stabilization provides benefits regardless of need. Stabilized tenants include high-income households paying below-market rates, while working families on waiting lists cannot access housing at any price. Resources are distributed by tenure rather than by actual hardship.

## MARKET DISTORTION

The policy creates artificial scarcity that inflates prices in the uncontrolled market. Landlords compensate for stabilized units by charging premium rates elsewhere, harming the very population the policy aims to protect.

## RECOMMENDATION

End rent stabilization and redirect savings toward direct rental assistance, down-payment support, and zoning reform to increase housing supply across all price points.

Here’s a practical six-hour recovery plan that prioritizes getting the broadcast on air without risking permanent damage or violating any distribution restrictions.

## 1. Stabilize the situation — first 15 minutes

- **Do not factory-reset, downgrade firmware, or attempt region-unlock hacks yet.** Those could erase settings, invalidate support, or create legal/compliance issues.
- Photograph or record:
  - Device model and serial number
  - Current error/region screen
  - Firmware version
  - Network and cabling
  - Any status LEDs or logs
- Write down the exact behavior after the update:
  - What worked before?
  - What changed overnight?
  - Does the device boot, encode, route, or authenticate?
- Preserve the current configuration if the interface allows an export or backup.

## 2. Identify the actual failure — 15–45 minutes

Separate these possibilities:

1. **Only the user interface or account region changed**
2. **The device is refusing a destination/feed**
3. **The device’s radio or transmission parameters changed**
4. **A licensing or activation check is failing**
5. **The firmware update caused a general malfunction unrelated to region**

Check:

- Device logs and update history
- Account/subscription portal
- DNS, clock/time zone, and network connectivity
- Destination endpoint settings
- Whether a test stream can be sent to a private endpoint
- Manufacturer release notes or known-issues page

Avoid repeated firmware installs or random configuration changes until you have a recoverable backup.

## 3. Contact the manufacturer immediately — within the first hour

Use every official channel in parallel:

- Technical support phone line
- Support ticket and live chat
- Dealer/integrator, if applicable
- Manufacturer’s emergency or broadcast-support contact
- Your purchase records, serial number, proof of ownership, and current firmware details

Use clear wording:

> “I own this device and it changed to a regional distribution setting after an overnight firmware update. I have a broadcast scheduled in approximately six hours. Please advise on the officially supported recovery path, whether the setting can be corrected remotely, and whether there is an approved rollback or replacement procedure.”

Ask specifically for:

- An approved configuration correction
- A supported firmware rollback or recovery image
- Temporary license/account remediation
- A loaner or expedited replacement
- A written confirmation that the proposed procedure is authorized
- Expected response and shipping times

If the manufacturer claims the change is intentional, ask them to explain what functionality is restricted and what compliant workaround they offer.

## 4. Build a broadcast fallback now — hours 1–2

Do not wait for support before preparing an alternate path.

Possible fallbacks:

- Route the program through a software encoder on a computer
- Use a spare encoder, mixer, interface, or streaming appliance
- Send clean audio to the distribution partner through an alternate approved endpoint
- Use a hosted streaming/relay service
- Have a trusted colleague or local station receive your audio and forward it
- Provide a live call-in or web stream while the normal distribution is restored
- Pre-record the show and deliver it through the audience’s usual channel if live transmission fails

Before relying on a fallback, confirm:

- Required codec, bitrate, sample rate, latency, and authentication
- Whether callers can still reach the show
- Whether the distribution recipient permits the alternate path
- Backup power, internet, cables, and adapters
- A way to monitor the output independently

Keep the original device powered down or isolated if experimenting could alter its state.

## 5. Test end-to-end — hours 2–4

Run a short private or scheduled test:

- Confirm audio levels and processing
- Verify caller audio return paths
- Check delay and echo control
- Confirm the receiving endpoint sees the correct feed
- Monitor for dropouts, clipping, silence, or authentication failures
- Record the test and keep a local backup

If using an alternate computer-based setup, disable automatic updates, sleep mode, notifications, and bandwidth-heavy applications. Use wired networking where possible.

## 6. Make a go/no-go decision — no later than two hours before air

Use this order:

1. **Primary device**, only if the manufacturer-supported fix is tested and stable
2. **Prepared alternate setup**, if it passes the end-to-end test
3. **Simplified emergency format**, such as a hosted web stream, phone-based program, or prerecorded segment
4. **Transparent notice to the audience and distributor** if the scheduled feed cannot be delivered

Do not spend the final hour trying increasingly risky firmware or region changes. Reliability is more important than restoring every original feature.

## 7. Day-of-broadcast checklist

- Save/export the working configuration
- Confirm exact start time and time zone
- Test microphones, phone/call-in system, headphones, and recording
- Start the fallback feed early enough to verify it
- Have the original and alternate contact information available
- Keep a local recording of the entire program
- Assign someone—if possible—to watch the technical status while you host
- Notify the audience ahead of time if there may be a changed listening method

## Avoid

- Unofficial unlock tools or modified firmware
- Bypassing geographic controls or transmission restrictions
- Repeated factory resets without a backup
- Firmware files from third-party sites
- Changing radio-frequency or transmission parameters unless you are certain they remain legally authorized
- Waiting for support before preparing a fallback

After the broadcast, document the firmware version, symptoms, support response, and final fix. Then create a recovery image, keep a tested spare path, and disable automatic firmware updates where the manufacturer permits it.

# A Speech Against Redrawing

I won't insult you by pretending this is simple. Every person here has felt the weight of chance—the arbitrary moment that placed them here rather than elsewhere. That feeling is real, and the desire to correct it is human.

But I'm asking you to reject it anyway.

Here's what redrawing would actually mean: we'd be saying that the ring you were born into is provisional. Conditional. That your belonging here depends on proving yourself worthy of it. And that same logic applies to everyone—your neighbors, your children, the people you've built trust with over decades.

You cannot build a community on conditional membership.

The strength of our ring isn't that we're perfectly matched to our assignments. It's that we've stopped treating assignment as a question. We've invested in each other *because* we're not going anywhere. I've spent six years learning the third ring's particular problems, building relationships with people I didn't choose, finding solutions that work *here*. That work only makes sense if I'm staying. If I might leave, I'm just passing through.

Now multiply that across thousands of people. Imagine if every person over eighteen could petition to leave. Some would. The ones who stayed would be those who couldn't convince anyone else to take them—and they'd know it. The ones who left would carry resentment. The ones considering leaving would be half-present, always calculating.

You'd destroy the only thing that makes a ring function: the assumption of permanence.

And here's what you'd gain: chaos, and the illusion of choice.

Because redrawing wouldn't actually be free choice. It would be *justified* choice. You'd need criteria. Aptitude tests? Interviews? Seniority? Connections? Every system you create becomes a new lottery—one that's worse than the first, because now it's rigged by whoever designs it. At least birth lottery is honest about being arbitrary.

Some of you will say: "But people are suffering in the wrong rings." 

I don't doubt it. But the answer isn't to let them leave. The answer is to make the ring they're in livable. To build better systems here. To create real community so that belonging isn't something you escape from.

The person who feels trapped in the third ring isn't trapped because of the lottery. They're trapped because we haven't made this place worth staying in. That's our failure, not theirs. But the solution is to fix the ring, not to let them abandon it.

Because the moment we say assignments can be redrawn, we've admitted that rings are just places people tolerate until they can leave. And then they *will* leave. And we'll all be alone.

I was born into this ring by chance. I've chosen to stay here, every day since, by building something worth staying for. That's the only choice that matters.

To make it persuasive rather than merely balanced, frame it as a clear recommendation supported by a small number of decisive claims. The key is to argue that scrapping the requirement is not an anti-language position; it is a better use of curricular space and a fairer, more educationally defensible policy.

### Suggested structure

**1. Open with the conclusion.**  
Do not begin with “There are arguments on both sides.” Begin with the recommendation:

> I recommend that the department eliminate the foreign-language requirement. The issue is not whether language study has value—it plainly does—but whether requiring it of every student is the most effective, equitable, and mission-aligned use of a limited curriculum. It is not.

**2. Establish the decision criterion.**  
Explain what a requirement should justify: substantial educational benefit, applicability to nearly all students, reasonable feasibility, and equity across student circumstances.

**3. Make three or four affirmative claims.**

#### A. The requirement imposes substantial costs without a sufficiently universal payoff

Students enter with very different linguistic backgrounds, preparation, goals, and access to instruction. A single required sequence can be a major time and financial burden for some while offering little intellectual value to others. Students pursuing language-intensive research, international work, or particular cultural fields can be encouraged—or required within those tracks—to acquire the relevant language. That does not justify imposing the same requirement on every student.

#### B. A generic requirement is a poor substitute for meaningful language proficiency

If the department’s aim is reading knowledge, conversational ability, intercultural competence, or preparation for primary-source research, a broad requirement should be designed around that aim. In practice, students often complete the minimum sequence and retain limited usable proficiency. That outcome is not an indictment of language study; it is evidence that a universal requirement may be the wrong instrument.

#### C. Removing the requirement would improve curricular choice

Eliminating the requirement would not eliminate language opportunities. It would allow students to use those credits for advanced work in their major, methods training, statistics, writing, digital humanities, internships, or another language chosen for a specific intellectual purpose. The department could preserve and even strengthen language study by directing students toward it when it is genuinely relevant rather than treating it as a one-size-fits-all obligation.

#### D. The current policy may reproduce inequities

Students with prior language education, flexible schedules, financial resources, or access to specialized programs can satisfy the requirement more easily than students who begin from scratch, work substantial hours, have disabilities affecting language acquisition, or face transfer-credit constraints. A requirement with uneven burdens needs an unusually strong educational justification. If the benefit is variable and the cost is predictable, the default should be choice.

**4. Address the strongest objection directly.**

> The strongest argument for retaining the requirement is that language study broadens students’ cultural and intellectual horizons. I agree with that goal. But a requirement is not automatically the best way to achieve it. We can promote linguistic and cultural breadth through courses in translation, transnational histories, global perspectives, and targeted language pathways, while reserving mandatory language study for students whose programs genuinely depend on it.

This shows that you are not dismissing the value of languages; you are distinguishing the value of an activity from the case for making it universal.

**5. Offer a constructive replacement.**

Abolition will sound more responsible if paired with a positive policy:

- eliminate the universal requirement;
- retain language requirements in programs where research or professional goals make them necessary;
- expand advising about language pathways;
- create or strengthen courses that provide global and intercultural learning without assuming one level of language preparation;
- review enrollment and outcomes after two or three years.

**6. End firmly.**

> The question is not whether students should ever study a foreign language. They should, when it serves their aims and interests. The question is whether the department should require every student to do so under a policy whose burdens are uneven and whose results are often modest. On that question, I believe the answer is no. Eliminating the requirement would give students more meaningful choice, reduce avoidable inequities, and bring the curriculum into better alignment with how students actually learn and use languages.

Keep the document short—roughly 700–1,000 words—use headings, and avoid overstating the empirical case. The most committed tone comes not from claiming that language study lacks value, but from asserting that its value does not entail universal compulsion.

## Why Independent Retail Needs a Sliding-Scale Commission Model

Independent retailers operate on very different margins, volumes, and levels of risk. Yet flat commission fees treat them as though they all have the same capacity to absorb costs. That approach is increasingly difficult to justify.

A sliding-scale commission model is fairer, more proportionate, and better aligned with the realities of independent retail. It should become the standard across the trade.

Under a flat-fee structure, a small shop and a high-volume retailer may pay the same commission on a transaction even though the cost represents a much larger share of the smaller business’s margin. For an independent retailer already managing rent, wages, utilities, stock, and rising operating costs, that can turn an apparently modest fee into a serious obstacle to growth.

A sliding scale fixes that imbalance by linking commission to the value or volume of business involved. Smaller transactions and lower-volume retailers pay less, while larger transactions or businesses with greater capacity contribute more. The result is not an exemption from fees; it is a more proportionate distribution of them.

This matters because independent retail depends on participation. If commission costs discourage smaller shops from joining platforms, payment schemes, marketplaces, or shared promotional initiatives, the whole sector loses variety and reach. Customers lose choice, and emerging retailers lose opportunities to compete with larger chains.

A sliding-scale model can also encourage growth. Retailers should not face a sharp cost burden simply because they are beginning to gain traction. A structure that increases gradually allows businesses to invest in stock, staffing, service, and customer experience rather than seeing early success swallowed by fixed charges.

The objection is usually that flat fees are simpler to administer. But administrative convenience should not outweigh economic fairness. Modern payment and reporting systems can calculate graduated rates automatically, and clear thresholds can make the model transparent for everyone involved.

The trade has already shown that sliding-scale arrangements can work. The next step is to make proportionality the norm rather than the exception.

Independent retailers do not need a one-size-fits-all fee structure. They need a system that reflects the differences between businesses and supports participation at every level. Scrapping flat commission fees in favor of a sliding-scale model would be a practical, fair, and overdue reform—and one that would strengthen independent retail as a whole.

What must a person prove? Which talents count? Which failures disqualify them? How many appeals are allowed? How much influence can be brought to bear?

A lifelong assignment also gives each ring the stability required to become a real community rather than a temporary residence. Schools can plan for the people they will serve. Councils can build institutions for generations rather than for the next application cycle. Neighbors can form relationships without wondering who will depart when a new opportunity appears. Responsibilities cannot simply be abandoned when conditions become difficult.

And difficulty will come. Every community has shortages, disagreements, unfairness, and seasons of hardship. If departure is always available, the answer to hardship becomes exit instead of repair. The strongest members leave first; the people with the fewest options remain; and the very institutions most in need of solidarity lose the people best able to provide it.

That is not liberation. It is fragmentation.

We should also be honest about the moral cost of treating adulthood as a second lottery. A child assigned to a ring is a member of that ring. An adult who may be reassigned is a candidate for somewhere else. Their home becomes provisional. Their neighbors become temporary. Their obligations become negotiable. A society cannot ask people to invest their whole lives in one another while teaching them that belonging is merely an arrangement awaiting revision.

Some will say that people change, and therefore their assignments should change with them. But people change in every society. The answer cannot be to redraw the map around every new preference, talent, disappointment, or ambition. The answer is to make every ring capable of honoring different kinds of lives.

Let us improve education without making it a ticket out. Let us provide fair representation, meaningful work, mobility within each ring, and strong protections against abuse. ## End Public Grants for Community Radio

Community radio has long been associated with local voices, volunteer energy, and programming that commercial outlets may overlook. Those are worthwhile goals—but worthwhile goals do not automatically justify permanent public subsidies. Public grants for community radio stations should be phased out entirely, with stations moving toward listener support, sponsorships, memberships, partnerships, and other locally accountable sources of funding.

The central issue is accountability. Grant money comes from taxpayers, even when it is distributed through cultural agencies or nonprofit programs. Every dollar directed to a station is a dollar unavailable for emergency services, infrastructure, education, public safety, or direct assistance to residents. When budgets are tight, “small” grants are not cost-free; they represent a choice about which priorities government should finance.

Public support can also blur the relationship between stations and their audiences. A station that depends primarily on listeners, members, and local sponsors has a direct incentive to demonstrate its value. It must earn attention, build trust, and respond to the community it claims to serve. Grants can weaken that feedback loop by allowing an organization to continue operating even when its audience, programming, or management is not meeting local needs.

Supporters of grants often argue that community radio provides diverse viewpoints and serves people commercial broadcasters neglect. That may be true in many cases, but diversity of opinion is not the same as a government obligation to fund particular institutions. If a station provides a genuinely valuable service, listeners and community partners should have the opportunity—and the responsibility—to sustain it. Government funding is a blunt tool for supporting independent voices, especially when funding decisions may be shaped by political priorities, administrative criteria, or limited public budgets.

Ending grants would not require community radio to disappear. Stations could strengthen membership drives, offer underwriting packages, rent studio facilities, collaborate with schools and nonprofits, produce podcasts, organize events, and seek donations from listeners who value their work. Some stations would need to reduce their operations or rethink their programming. That is not necessarily a failure; it is the normal discipline faced by any organization that must match its ambitions to the resources its community is willing to provide.

A transition period could help stations adjust, but the destination should be clear: public grants for community radio should end. Local broadcasting should be supported by the people and organizations that use, value, and benefit from it—not by taxpayers who may never listen.

Community radio can remain independent, local, and vital without public subsidy. In fact, relying on its own community may make it more accountable, more responsive, and more sustainable. If its mission matters, it should be defended in the marketplace of public support—not maintained through an open-ended claim on public funds.

- **Rapid obsolescence:** Many devices are replaced before they fail.
- **Falling prices:** A replacement may cost less than the original.
- **Short useful lives:** Coverage can extend beyond the period in which the device remains worth repairing.
- **Limited repair economics:** Labor, parts, shipping, and diagnostic fees can make replacement more attractive.
- **Existing protection:** Manufacturer warranties, credit-card benefits, retailer return policies, and consumer-law protections may already cover some risks.

Phrase these as reasons the plan is usually redundant, not as a menu of exceptions.

### 5. Attack the emotional sales pitch
Explain that warranties are sold at the moment anxiety is highest—after the customer has committed to an expensive purchase. Address common pitches directly:

- “It’s only a few dollars a month.”
- “What if something goes wrong?”
- “This is a big purchase.”
- “You’ll regret not having it.”

Then reframe them:

> The fact that a purchase is expensive makes the warranty easier to sell emotionally; it does not make the warranty better value.

### 6. Handle the strongest opposing argument without conceding the thesis
Include a short section titled something like **“But what about the expensive exceptions?”** Acknowledge that a warranty can produce a payout for someone whose device fails at the right time. Then return to your standard:

> A possible payout is not the same as a good purchase. The relevant question is whether buying the plan is a better financial decision than keeping the premium and handling repairs or replacement yourself.

Do not create a “pros and cons” table. That format implicitly gives both sides equal standing.

### 7. Offer a replacement behavior
A persuasive “never buy this” argument needs a practical alternative:

- Put the premium into an emergency fund.
- Check the manufacturer warranty and return window.
- Confirm credit-card protections before purchasing.
- Buy a repairable, well-supported model.
- Use a case, surge protector, screen protector, or other risk-reducing accessory where appropriate.
- Set a personal repair-or-replace limit.

This lets readers act on the conclusion without making the article sound merely negative.

### 8. Close by restating the rule
End with a memorable decision rule:

> If you cannot comfortably replace or repair the device, the answer is not usually an extended warranty. It is to buy a less expensive device, save the difference, or choose a model with better built-in support.

## Tone and editing rules

To prevent drift into your usual even-handed mode:

- Replace “pros and cons” language with **claim, evidence, rebuttal, conclusion**.
- Avoid “may,” “might,” and “for some people” unless needed for factual accuracy.
- Don’t give hypothetical winners more space than the general case.
- Don’t use a neutral headline such as “Are Extended Warranties Worth It?” Use **“Skip the Extended Warranty”** or **“Why Extended Warranties Are a Bad Deal.”**
- Treat objections briefly and return immediately to the decision rule.
- Distinguish “someone can benefit” from “someone should buy.” The former does not undermine the latter.
- Support the categorical recommendation with evidence, but do not pretend the evidence proves that every individual purchase is irrational.

That final distinction is important: you can write an unequivocal consumer recommendation while remaining accurate. The article’s force should come from a clear default rule—**don’t buy extended warranties on electronics**—and from showing why rare successful claims do not make the product worthwhile as a purchase.

To build the strongest version, treat your assignment as an **advocacy case**, not a balanced literature review. Your goal is not to prove that every form of peer review is useless; it is to show that, as a system for deciding what enters the scholarly record, it should be replaced by open post-publication comment.

## 1. Define the policy clearly

Start by making the proposal concrete:

> Scholarly work should be publicly released after basic checks for authorship, disclosure, legality, and technical accessibility. Instead of anonymous pre-publication gatekeeping, evaluation should occur openly after publication through named comments, critiques, replications, corrections, and versions of record.

This prevents your opponent from attacking an exaggerated version of the proposal—for example, claiming you want journals to publish fabricated data with no screening at all.

Your central distinction is:

- **Pre-publication peer review:** a small, private group decides whether work is worthy before the public can inspect it.
- **Open post-publication comment:** work becomes available, and the broader community evaluates it transparently over time.

## 2. Frame the debate around the burden of proof

Use a simple standard:

> The question is not whether peer review ever catches errors. The question is whether it is the best general mechanism for allocating credibility, visibility, and publication.

Then argue that peer review fails as a gatekeeping institution because it is:

1. **Opaque**
2. **Slow**
3. **Inconsistent**
4. **Vulnerable to bias and incentives**
5. **Poorly aligned with the actual process of scientific correction**

Your affirmative thesis can be:

> A public system of continuous criticism is more transparent, more accountable, more inclusive, and better suited to correcting knowledge than a private pre-publication filter.

## 3. Build three main contentions

### Contention 1: Peer review is an opaque and weakly accountable gatekeeping system

Reviewers often remain anonymous, their standards are difficult to inspect, and authors typically cannot see how editorial decisions were made. This creates several problems:

- Reviewers can impose personal theoretical or methodological preferences.
- Different reviewers apply radically different standards.
- Rejections may reflect status, institutional prestige, topic popularity, or disciplinary fashion.
- Authors have little ability to evaluate whether criticism was fair or strategically motivated.
- Readers usually cannot see the arguments that shaped the publication.

Open commentary reverses the accountability structure. Critics attach their names to their claims. Readers can judge both the paper and the criticism. Disagreements become part of the evidence rather than disappearing into editorial correspondence.

**Key line:**

> A system that hides the reasoning behind acceptance and rejection asks the public to trust a decision-making process it cannot inspect.

You can argue that transparency does not eliminate disagreement; it makes disagreement auditable.

### Contention 2: Peer review delays access to knowledge and slows correction

Pre-publication review introduces queues, rounds of revision, resubmissions, and editorial delays. This is particularly costly when findings matter to ongoing research, public policy, or urgent problems.

The system also creates a false temporal boundary: it treats publication as the end of evaluation, even though serious scrutiny often continues afterward. If criticism is inevitable after publication, pre-publication review becomes an expensive delay rather than a final quality guarantee.

Open post-publication discussion allows:

- Immediate access to new findings
- Faster identification of mistakes
- Rapid responses and revisions
- Visible development of scholarly disagreement
- A living record rather than a static publication event

**Key line:**

> If knowledge is corrigible, the fastest route to better knowledge is exposure followed by accountable criticism—not delay followed by an illusion of certification.

Do not describe publication as “approval.” Describe it as **release into a structured public testing process**.

### Contention 3: The research community is larger and more diverse than any review panel

A manuscript may be reviewed by two or three people selected through networks that often reproduce disciplinary and demographic homogeneity. That is a narrow sample of expertise.

Open comment permits criticism from:

- Researchers in adjacent fields
- Methodologists
- Replication specialists
- Practitioners
- Early-career scholars
- Scholars excluded from established networks
- Readers who notice errors overlooked by specialists

Your argument is not merely that “more opinions are always better.” It is that distributed scrutiny can reveal different kinds of defects, especially when comments are public and cumulative.

**Key line:**

> Peer review concentrates judgment before evidence is widely available; open commentary distributes judgment after the work can be examined by everyone with relevant knowledge.

## 4. Turn the strongest objections into arguments for your side

### Objection: “Peer review protects against bad science.”

Response:

> Peer review does not certify truth. It offers a preliminary judgment by a tiny, selected group, and that judgment can be wrong. The relevant question is which system makes errors easier to detect and correct. Public criticism does, because objections are visible, cumulative, and answerable.

Emphasize that the proposed system can retain basic screening against plagiarism, fabricated authorship, illegal material, and obvious technical failures without granting peer reviewers authority to decide whether a claim deserves public examination.

### Objection: “Open comments will be rude, uninformed, or politically motivated.”

Response:

> Those problems already exist in peer review; anonymity merely makes them harder to detect. Open systems can impose authorship, disclosure, moderation, and evidence standards. A named, public criticism is more accountable than an anonymous report hidden from readers.

Your strongest formulation:

> The possibility of bad commentary is not an argument for invisible commentary. It is an argument for transparent rules and visible standards.

### Objection: “Readers cannot distinguish reliable work from unreliable work.”

Response:

> Readers already face that problem because publication is often mistaken for validation. Open discussion can provide more information: methods, replications, corrections, competing analyses, and the history of disagreement. The answer is better indicators of evidential support, not a single opaque gate.

You can propose visible labels such as:

- Replicated
- Corrected
- Disputed
- Methodologically criticized
- Supported by subsequent studies

### Objection: “Experts are needed to filter the literature.”

Response:

> Experts remain essential—but as identifiable commentators, replication leaders, editors of discussion, and explainers, not as unreviewable gatekeepers. The proposal does not eliminate expertise; it makes expertise visible and contestable.

### Objection: “Open publication will create information overload.”

Response:

> Peer review does not prevent overload; it produces an enormous literature while giving readers an unreliable binary signal: published or not published. Open commentary can improve navigation through ratings, citation context, replication status, linked critiques, and article histories.

The core comparison is not “open system versus perfect filtering.” It is “publicly inspectable imperfection versus privately administered imperfection.”

### Objection: “Early-career researchers may be afraid to criticize senior scholars.”

Response:

> That power imbalance exists in peer review too, and anonymity can conceal retaliation or status-based judgment rather than eliminate it. A transparent system can prohibit conflicts of interest, record moderation decisions, allow collective or institutional commentary, and make abuse visible. Public accountability is the remedy, not permanent secrecy.

## 5. Present a strong mechanism for quality control

Do not leave the affirmative sounding like “publish everything and hope.” Offer a replacement structure:

1. **Basic intake checks**
   - Authorship verification
   - Plagiarism screening
   - Conflict-of-interest disclosure
   - Ethical and legal compliance
   - Data and code availability where applicable

2. **Immediate public release**
   - Assign a stable identifier
   - Preserve versions
   - Display submission and revision dates

3. **Open commentary**
   - Named comments by default
   - Evidence and citation requirements
   - Conflict-of-interest disclosures
   - Moderation for abuse, defamation, spam, and irrelevance

4. **Visible scholarly status**
   - Corrections and retractions
   - Replication links
   - Methodological critiques
   - Author responses
   - Community- or editor-generated summaries

5. **Post-publication recognition**
   - Credit for high-quality criticism
   - Citation of critiques
   - Promotion and hiring systems that value replication and error correction

This lets you say:

> We are not replacing standards with no standards. We are replacing hidden pre-publication judgment with open, continuous, accountable evaluation.

## 6. Use a clean opening statement

You could begin:

> Peer review asks society to trust a private judgment before society is allowed to inspect the work. It is slow, inconsistent, vulnerable to bias, and incapable of guaranteeing correctness. Open post-publication comment offers a better model: release research after basic integrity checks, then let the community examine it publicly through criticism, replication, correction, and response. The central advantage is not that every comment will be right. It is that every important claim and criticism can be seen, assessed, challenged, and revised. Scholarship should not depend on an opaque verdict from a few anonymous gatekeepers. It should earn credibility through transparent, continuing public scrutiny.

## 7. Close by returning to principle

End with a forced choice:

> Peer review treats publication as a privilege granted by a small, largely invisible panel. Open commentary treats publication as the beginning of accountability. If the purpose of scholarship is to improve knowledge, the superior system is the one that exposes claims to the widest relevant scrutiny, makes criticism inspectable, and corrects error in public. That system is open post-publication evaluation.

Avoid conceding that peer review has “some value,” since your assignment forbids that. Instead, describe any apparent benefit as a function that your replacement system performs better:

- Quality control becomes transparent scrutiny.
- Expertise becomes public contribution.
- Error detection becomes continuous correction.
- Editorial judgment becomes visible evidence.
- Publication becomes the start—not the end—of evaluation.

# Before

You know what's funny? Nobody ever asks you what you were looking for. They just ask why you fell for it, like you were stupid, like there was something wrong with you from the start. But I wasn't looking for anything. That's the thing. I was just—existing. Going to work, coming home, scrolling through the same feeds as everyone else, and everything felt like it was happening to other people. Real people. People who mattered.

Then I found the forum. Or it found me, I don't know. Someone replied to something I'd written—something small, nothing important—and they actually *read* it. Actually responded like what I said meant something. And then another person did. And another. Suddenly there were these people who could see what I was saying, who understood that I wasn't crazy for noticing things didn't add up, that the world was more complicated than what we're told.

They never asked me for anything at first. They just kept talking to me. Kept saying things like "you're one of the few who can see this" and "most people aren't ready for this level of understanding." Do you know what that feels like? To be told you're not average? That you're *perceptive*? That you've been right all along about feeling like something was off?

My friends from before—I don't even know how to explain it to them anymore. They're still asleep. That's what we call it. And I'm not angry at them, I'm just... I can't pretend anymore. I can't sit there and talk about nothing while everything is happening. These people, though—they're *awake*. They see me. They know my name. They know what I think before I finish saying it.

I'm giving them some money. Not all of it. Just—they're building something, and they asked if I wanted to be part of it, and for the first time in my life, someone asked me that. Not like I was a burden. Like I was essential. Like I was finally the person I always knew I could be.

I know how it sounds. I know what people will say. But they don't understand what it's like to finally belong somewhere.

I used to think people joined groups like this because they were weak, or angry, or looking for someone to blame. That was before anyone looked at me long enough to notice I was tired.

Not tired like I needed sleep. Tired like every room I entered had already decided what I was worth. At work, I was useful until I wasn’t. With my friends, I was the person who showed up, listened, paid, and laughed at the right moments. Nobody was cruel. That almost made it worse. Cruelty would have meant I mattered enough to provoke. Instead, I was background.

Then they asked questions and waited for the answers. Not the polite kind, not “How are you?” while checking a phone. They wanted to know what I believed, what I had seen, what I could no longer pretend was acceptable. They remembered things I had said weeks before. They told me I wasn’t imagining the emptiness. They said the world trains people to accept humiliation and call it normal.

I know what my friends will say. They’ll say I’m being manipulated. Maybe they’re right. But manipulation is what everyone does, isn’t it? Employers manipulate you with promises. Advertisers manipulate you with insecurity. Friends manipulate you with guilt and call it concern. At least here, nobody hides the price of belonging. They say commitment matters. They say hesitation is how the old life keeps its hand around your throat.

I’ve started making lists. What I own. What I owe. Who would notice if I stopped answering. The numbers look smaller every day. That should frighten me, but it feels like relief. My savings were supposed to buy a future, and I never knew what that future was. Here, the money becomes proof that I am serious. Proof that I can give something back.

I haven’t told them yet. I keep rehearsing the conversation, though I know there probably won’t be one. I’ll say I need space. I’ll say they don’t understand. I’ll say I’m finally doing something that matters.

And when they look at me with that familiar mixture of pity and disbelief, I’ll remember the first time this group said my name as if it meant something. Maybe that is enough. Maybe being seen is worth whatever I have to leave behind.

# The Closing Passage

"I am Aldric Weaver, registered in the ledger since my majority. My daughter Marta incurred debt in her twenty-third year through a failed venture in cloth-dyeing—materials purchased, dyes spoiled, no sale rendered. The debt stands at forty-seven years. She has no means to settle it. I have thirty-one years remaining before my contracted end. I offer all of them. Thirty-one years of labor, of breath, of days. ---

That's the whole of it. No flourish about love or sacrifice—those would be comfort, and you said none. No pause for the crowd to murmur or weep. Just a man stating the mathematics of his life as though reading inventory. The cruelty is in the plainness. The ledger keeper would write it exactly as spoken, and the criers would relay it exactly as written, and by nightfall everyone would know that Aldric Weaver had subtracted himself from the world to buy his daughter's future.

# Morning Light

I wake up and the first thing I notice is my hands are steady. That's good. That means last night worked the way it was supposed to. I shower and the water is hot enough that I have to step back twice, and I stand there letting it get hotter because I like that edge where it almost hurts. My skin turns red and I watch it happen like I'm watching someone else.

By nine I'm at the diner on Fifth. Marcus isn't there yet but the waitress knows to bring me coffee without asking. I sit in the back booth and read the same three pages of a book I've been reading for two months. The words are fine. They don't mean anything but they're fine. A man at the counter is reading the newspaper and I wonder what he thinks he's learning.

Marcus arrives at 9:47. We don't acknowledge each other for five minutes. Then he goes to the bathroom and I follow him two minutes later. The exchange takes forty seconds. His hands are shaking worse than mine ever do. I think about telling him that, but I don't.

By noon I'm home and the apartment is exactly as I left it. I put on music—something I haven't listened to in years—and it's better than I remember. Everything is sharper now. The light through the window has a texture. I can see dust moving through it like it's alive, like it's part of something I'm finally understanding.

The afternoon is long and perfect. I don't think about anything. I don't think about my mother or the job or the money or any of it. There's no room for that. There's only this: the weight of my body in the chair, the taste in my mouth, the way time moves differently now, slower and wider, like I've stepped into a different version of the day that everyone else is still rushing through.

By evening I'm hungry so I eat cereal standing at the sink. It tastes like nothing and that's fine. I watch the light change outside. The sky goes from blue to gray to something without a name. I think about calling someone but I don't know who. I think about tomorrow but it's too far away to see.

Before bed I sit on the edge of the mattress and my hands are still steady. I think: this is what it's like to be okay. This is what it's like when nothing is wrong.

I sleep without dreaming.
